newsitem.title: USA: Dole gets tough in debate; Clinton smiles through it.
newsitem.headline: Dole gets tough in debate; Clinton smiles through it.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Republican Bob Dole on Wednesday accused President Bill Clinton of running an unethical administration but the president smiled through the onslaught in the final campaign debate, appearing confident he is headed for re-election.

In a 90-minute town hall meeting with questions from an audience of undecided oters, Dole went straight on the offensive, lashing out at Clinton's ethics, credibility and performance and blaming him for Americans losing faith in government.
"They see scandals almost on a daily basis. They see ethical problems in the White House today. They see 900 FBI files, private person, being gathered up somebody in the White House," he said.

Clinton, whose lead in opinion polls released on Wednesday ranged from nine to 17 points with less than three weeks left until Election Day on Nov. 5, stuck to the achievements of his four years in office, showing cool command of his arguments.

Three snap polls showed a large majority saw Clinton as the winner. In an ABC poll, 56 percent of respondents said the president had won while 27 percent said Dole had won. A CBS poll gave the victory to Clinton 55 percent to 25 percent and CNN had the president winning 59 to 29 percent.

Some voters said Dole was too harsh. "What are people going to remember about this? Dole said a lot of bad things about Clinton and Clinton didn't break a sweat," said Buddy Wilson, owner of a sports bar in Daytona Beach, Florida, where tv sets were divided between the debate and a baseball game.
"Clinton talked a lot of policy and nobody's going to remember any of that tomorrow, but they'll remember how calm he looked," he said.

Ann Regal, a special education teacher in New Smyrna Beach, Florida, said: "Dole was very negative throughout and I think that hurt him. He'd start every answer with an attack on the president and that's all you wanted to listen to -- how dirty will he get this time?"
Dole returned to the ethical question at least twice more, both times without provoking any reaction from Clinton.

"When you're the president of the United States, you have a public trust," Dole said. "And you have to keep that public trust ... And I think now that trust is being violated, and it seems to me we ought to face up to it."
Later Dole said Clinton had an "ethics problem" because 30 members of his administration were in jail or under investigation. Again the president offered no response.
The candidates' responses after the debate told the story. Asked how he thought he had performed, Dole told reporters: "I showed up." Asked if he won, Dole replied: "I don't know."
Clinton went to a rally of some 10,000 people in San Diego where the mood was euphoric and shook dozens of hands of ecstatic supporters.
Clinton showed his mastery of the town hall format, frequently moving to within inches of the audience, embracing them with expansive gestures. Dole, more reserved, stayed closer to the podium.
Political analysts told Reuters Dole did well, but Clinton did what was necessary to protect his lead.

"Dole didn't go for the jugular. He inflicted a couple of flesh wounds but Clinton will put on a couple of band-aids and it will be over," said John Pitney, a political scientist at Claremont McKenna College in California.
Beverly Wall, a professor of rhetoric at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, said Dole had by far the more difficult task of attacking Clinton without seeming too harsh.

"Clinton never took the bait and he clearly showed his analytical skills, focusing on answering the question. He played it safe, though those who don't like him will probably say he was too smooth," she said.

Dole seemed to stumble when he was asked whether tobacco was addictive. "Are they (cigarettes) addictive? Maybe -- they probably are addictive. I don't know. I'm not a doctor. You shouldn't smoke. You ought to be glad you quit," he said to the questioner who kicked a pack-a-day habit.
Clinton said he was the first president to take on the tobacco lobby and that Dole had opposed him.
When not going after Clinton's ethics, Dole tried to discredit Clinton's claims of a strong economy.

"That's a good economy? I don't think so. They're setting new records this year. We have the worst economy in a century. We've had the slowest growth, about 2.5 percent. The president inherited a growth of over 5 percent," he said.
Clinton quickly seized on the comment: "Senator Dole just said we had the worst economy in a century. In February he said we had the best economy in 30 years."

Asked by a student how at age 73 he could understand the needs of young people, Dole responded with a joke. "You know, wisdom comes from age, experience and intelligence. And if you have some of each -- and I have some age and some experience, some intelligence -- that adds up to wisdom. I think it also is a strength. It's an advantage."
Clinton came right back at his challenger: "I can only tell you that I don't think Senator Dole is too old to be president. It's the age of his ideas that I question."

It was not yet known how many people watched the debate. The TV audience for the first debate was estimated at about 46 million viewers, 34 percent fewer than watched the comparable 1992 debate. Wednesday's event competed against a baseball playoff game on one network.
